what_it_shows: Real Adrian Shoe Fitter, Inc. fluoroscope, c. 1938, used in a Washington, D.C. shoe store. Wood cabinet with three viewing hoods on top (child, parent, salesperson), control knob, timer slot, meter. 768x1024, a little soft.
best_segments: S2 how it worked (three viewing hoods)

credit_line: Photo: Maury Markowitz / CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: Decommissioned later-model Adrian Fluoroscope at the Dufferin County Museum, Ontario: three black rubber viewing hoods on top, the operator's control panel and a meter. 3264x2448, sharp.
best_segments: S2 how it worked (close-up on the three viewing ports)

credit_line: Photo: Andrew Kuchling / CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: Adrian shoe-fitting X-ray device on museum display in St. Paul, Minnesota (2001), seen from the customer's side: a tall center eyepiece and two side hoods. Museum cards read 'Shoe Fitting X-Ray Device', 'Seized by the U.S. Food & Drug Adm.' and 'Not Plugged in - Illegal to Operate!'. Do NOT use the FDA card as evidence; crop it or keep it unreadable.
best_segments: S4 result ('Illegal to Operate' card, if legible)

credit_line: Photo: Roxane Poudenas & Léo Lespets, Musée des Hospices Civils de Lyon / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: British Pedoscope Company machine (1924–1950) on a white studio background, seen from the front: the foot opening at the bottom and three viewing hoods on top. 2731x4096, very clean, easy to cut out.
best_segments: S2 how it worked (foot slot at bottom, three hoods on top)

credit_line: Photo: Roxane Poudenas & Léo Lespets, Musée des Hospices Civils de Lyon / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: Close-up of the brass maker's plate, 'THE PEDOSCOPE COMPANY 118-120 HOLBORN LONDON E.C.1', on walnut wood.

credit_line: Photo: Roxane Poudenas & Léo Lespets, Musée des Hospices Civils de Lyon / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: Side profile of the same Pedoscope: a slanted cabinet with the foot step at the bottom right and viewing hoods on top. Useful silhouette for the diagram.

license: Public domain (U.S. patent 1,614,988, published Jan. 18, 1927; U.S. publication before 1931)
credit_line: J. J. Lowe, U.S. Patent 1,614,988 (1927) / Public domain
what_it_shows: Jacob J. Lowe's patent, 'Method and Means for Visually Determining the Fit of Footwear' (filed 1919, granted 1927). Fig. 2 is a CUTAWAY: the X-ray tube (2) and transformer (3) in the base, under the foot opening (15), and a viewing hood (11/12) rising up to the eye of a dotted standing figure. 2320x3408 line art.

license: Public domain (U.S. design patent D149,088, 1948; U.S. patent drawings are generally not subject to copyright and this sheet carries no copyright notice). Lower confidence than the pre-1931 items.
credit_line: J. O. Reinecke, U.S. Design Patent D149,088 (1948) / Public domain
what_it_shows: 'X-Ray Shoe Fitting Cabinet' design patent, two perspective views of a streamlined late-1940s cabinet with three viewing hoods and a foot slot. Black bar at the bottom; crop it.

license: Public domain (published 1912 in the U.S.; work of a U.S. Army officer)
credit_line: E. L. Munson, The Soldier's Foot and the Military Shoe (1912) / Public domain
what_it_shows: Real X-ray of a foot inside a shoe: toe bones with the shoe outline around them ('a perfect fit'). Plate label 'I.51' in the corner. This is a 1912 Army radiograph, NOT a shoe-store fluoroscope screen.
best_segments: S2 'toe bones' (green-tint it to look like a fluorescent screen; label it 'X-ray of a foot in a shoe, 1912')

license: Public domain (published 1912 in the U.S.; work of a U.S. Army officer)
credit_line: E. L. Munson, The Soldier's Foot and the Military Shoe (1912) / Public domain
what_it_shows: X-ray of the same foot in a pointed garrison shoe. The phalanges are clearly visible inside the shoe outline. Label 'I.47'.
best_segments: S3 (pulse or flash to suggest a dose)

license: Public domain (published 1912 in the U.S.; work of a U.S. Army officer)
credit_line: E. L. Munson, The Soldier's Foot and the Military Shoe (1912) / Public domain
what_it_shows: X-ray of a foot crammed into a shoe that is too short and too narrow. Blurrier than the others.

license: Public domain (published 1920 in the U.S. by U.S. Navy officers; Flickr Commons 'No known copyright restrictions')
credit_line: Mann & Folsom, A Manual on Foot Care and Shoe Fitting for Officers of the U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps (1920) / Public domain, via Internet Archive Book Images
what_it_shows: High-contrast X-ray of a foot inside a shoe, with a black 'Resco' shoe-fitting device in the toe cavity. Toe bones and the shoe outline are crisp, but the black plug is distracting.

credit_line: Boston Public Library / CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: Linen postcard (about 1930–1945) of the storefront of 'Scientific Shoe Fitters', 570 Bloomfield Ave., Bloomfield, N.J. Nothing shows this store had a fluoroscope, so use it only as generic period shoe-store B-roll.

license: Public domain (PD-US-expired: published in the U.S. Dec. 8, 1928)
credit_line: Boot and Shoe Recorder, Dec. 8, 1928 / Public domain
what_it_shows: Trade-magazine page 'Know the Foot' with an anatomical foot cross-section. It is not a fluoroscope ad, and at 330x477 it is too small for full-frame use.
